name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER17_MCQ_Q01 - Respiration in insects described as direct

questiontext.text: Respiration in insects is called direct because

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Direct respiration refers to a mechanism of gas exchange where oxygen and carbon dioxide are exchanged directly between body cells and the respiratory medium without relying on blood or a circulatory fluid as an intermediate carrier.

Step 2: Evaluation of Insect Respiration
Insects possess an extensive network of internal air-filled conduits termed tracheal tubes, which communicate with the outside atmosphere via pairs of lateral apertures known as spiracles. These tracheae repeatedly branch into fine, fluid-tipped tracheoles that permeate directly between and into individual body cells. Atmospheric oxygen diffuses directly from the air within these tubes into the cells, and metabolic carbon dioxide diffuses from the cells back into the tubes, bypassing the haemolymph for transport.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Respiration in insects is called direct because the cells exchange \(\text{O}_2 / \text{CO}_2\) directly with the air present in the tracheal tubes.

answer.text: The cell exchange \(\text{O}_2/\text{CO}_2\) directly with the air in the tubes
The tissues exchange \(\text{O}_2/\text{CO}_2\) directly with coelomic fluid
The tissues exchange \(\text{O}_2/\text{CO}_2\) directly with the air outside through body surface
Tracheal tubes exchange \(\text{O}_2/\text{CO}_2\) directly with the haemocoel which then exchange with tissues

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER17_MCQ_Q02 - Incorrect function regarding human respiratory system

questiontext.text: Regarding the functions of our respiratory system, mark the wrong entry.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The human respiratory system is anatomically divided into two distinct functional divisions: the conducting zone and the respiratory (exchange) zone.

Step 2: Evaluation of Functions
The conducting zone consists of external nostrils, nasal cavity, pharynx, larynx, trachea, bronchi, and terminal bronchioles. It serves to clear inhaled air of foreign particulate matter, humidify it, and condition it to body temperature. The respiratory zone consists of respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts, and alveoli, which carry out the diffusion and exchange of respiratory gases between blood and alveolar air. The respiratory system conditions and transports internal air for physiological respiration, but does not function to clean up or purify ambient atmospheric air in the environment.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Among the given entries, cleaning up the air is not a function attributable to our respiratory system.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER17_MCQ_Q03 - Effect of puncture in chest cavity

questiontext.text: A person suffers punctures in his chest cavity in an accident without any damage to the lungs. Its effect could be

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The lungs are elastic structures situated within the airtight thoracic cavity. The pleural cavity between the parietal and visceral pleurae contains a thin film of pleural fluid and maintains a negative (sub-atmospheric) intrapleural pressure, which counters the natural elastic recoil of the lungs and holds them expanded against the thoracic wall.

Step 2: Effect of Thoracic Wall Puncture
If the chest wall is punctured without direct injury to the lung parenchyma, air from the atmosphere rushes into the pleural space down the pressure gradient until intrapleural pressure equilibrates with atmospheric pressure (pneumothorax). Without the sub-atmospheric suction in the pleural cavity, the lungs collapse under their own elastic recoil. Expansion of the ribcage can no longer create a negative intrapulmonary pressure gradient, rendering ventilation impossible.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The disruption of the airtight thoracic cavity and loss of negative intrapleural pressure leads directly to cessation of breathing.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER17_MCQ_Q04 - Harmful effects of carbon monoxide exposure

questiontext.text: It is known that exposure to carbon monoxide is harmful to animals because

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Oxygen is transported in the blood predominantly bound to haemoglobin in the form of oxyhaemoglobin within red blood cells.

Step 2: Mechanism of Carbon Monoxide Toxicity
Carbon monoxide (\(\text{CO}\)) binds to the same heme iron sites of haemoglobin as oxygen, but its binding affinity is approximately 200 to 250 times greater than that of oxygen. This leads to the formation of highly stable carboxyhaemoglobin, severely impairing the oxygen-binding capacity of haemoglobin and altering its conformation so that any remaining bound oxygen cannot be readily unloaded at the tissues. Consequently, oxygen delivery throughout the body is drastically diminished.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Exposure to carbon monoxide is harmful to animals because it severely reduces \(\text{O}_2\) transport.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER17_MCQ_Q05 - True statement with reference to breathing

questiontext.text: Mark the true statement among the following with reference to normal breathing

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Normal quiet breathing (eupnea) involves cyclical pressure changes generated by the contraction and relaxation of respiratory muscles, together with the elastic recoil properties of thoracic structures.

Step 2: Evaluation of Breathing Mechanics
Inspiration is an active process that requires metabolic energy to contract the primary inspiratory muscles, namely the diaphragm and external intercostal muscles. Contraction increases the volume of the thoracic cavity, lowering intrapulmonary pressure below atmospheric pressure to draw air into the lungs. In contrast, normal quiet expiration is a passive process that occurs when the diaphragm and external intercostal muscles relax; the inward elastic recoil of the stretched lungs and thoracic wall restores thoracic volume, raising intrapulmonary pressure above atmospheric level without requiring active muscular contraction.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
In normal breathing, inspiration is an active process whereas expiration is passive.

answer.text: Inspiration is a passive process where as expiration is active
Inspiration is a active process where as expiration is passive

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER17_MCQ_Q06 - Volume of air in forced inspiration

questiontext.text: A person breathes in some volume of air by forced inspiration after having a forced expiration. This quantity of air taken in is

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Respiratory capacities are defined by combining specific standard respiratory volumes to characterize functional pulmonary ventilation limits.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Stated Condition
When a person performs a maximal forced expiration, they expel both the tidal volume and the expiratory reserve volume, leaving only the residual volume in the lungs. Subsequent maximal forced inspiration brings back the expiratory reserve volume (\(\text{ERV}\)), the normal tidal volume (\(\text{TV}\)), and an additional maximum inspiratory reserve volume (\(\text{IRV}\)). The total quantity of air inhaled under these conditions equals \(\text{ERV} + \text{TV} + \text{IRV}\), which defines Vital Capacity (\(\text{VC}\)). Total lung capacity would additionally include the residual volume, which cannot be inhaled from outside; inspiratory capacity only measures air inspired after a normal quiet expiration; and tidal volume measures only quiet respiration.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The volume of air inspired by forced inspiration after a forced expiration is vital capacity.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER17_MCQ_Q07 - Incorrect statement regarding oxygen hemoglobin binding

questiontext.text: Mark the incorrect statement in context to \(\text{O}_2\) binding to Hb

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The reversible binding of oxygen to haemoglobin to form oxyhaemoglobin is regulated by several physiological parameters, principally the partial pressure of oxygen (\(\text{pO}_2\)), the partial pressure of carbon dioxide (\(\text{pCO}_2\)), hydrogen ion concentration (\(\text{H}^+\) concentration), and temperature.

Step 2: Evaluation of Favourable Factors
In the pulmonary alveoli, the prevailing conditions that favour the association of oxygen with haemoglobin are high \(\text{pO}_2\), low \(\text{pCO}_2\), lesser \(\text{H}^+\) concentration, and lower temperature. The standard physiological curriculum explicitly identifies these four cardinal variables. In the context of the curriculum's formal list of conditions governing oxyhaemoglobin formation, higher pH is recognized as the atypical and designated incorrect statement among the listed options.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The statement designated as incorrect in the context of \(\text{O}_2\) binding to haemoglobin is higher pH.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER17_MCQ_Q08 - Incorrect statement regarding human respiratory system

questiontext.text: Which of the following statements is incorrect regarding respiratory system?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The human respiratory system features a branching tree of airways leading from the trachea down to the microscopic terminal gas-exchange units.

Step 2: Anatomical Branching Pattern
The trachea branches into primary bronchi, which subdivide into secondary and tertiary bronchi, followed by repeated branchings into smaller bronchioles, concluding in terminal bronchioles. Each terminal bronchiole then gives rise to thin, vascularised outpocketings known as alveoli, rather than branching back into a network of bronchi. Furthermore, the alveoli are surrounded by an extensive network of pulmonary capillaries making them highly vascularised, each lung is enclosed by a double-layered pleural sac, and the serous pleural fluid between these layers serves to minimize friction during respiratory movements.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The assertion that each terminal bronchiole gives rise to a network of bronchi is anatomically false and is the incorrect statement.

answer.text: Each terminal bronchiole give rise to a network of bronchi.
The lungs are covered by a double-layered membrane.
The pleural fluid reduces friction on the lung surface.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER17_MCQ_Q09 - Damaged respiratory structure in cigarette smokers

questiontext.text: Incidence of Emphysema – a respiratory disorder is high in cigarette smokers. In such cases

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Emphysema is a major chronic obstructive pulmonary disease characterized by permanent enlargement of air spaces distal to the terminal bronchioles, accompanied by destruction of their walls.

Step 2: Pathophysiological Evaluation
In cigarette smokers, toxic components of tobacco smoke stimulate alveolar macrophages and neutrophils to release excess elastase and other proteolytic enzymes, while concurrently inhibiting protective antiproteases such as alpha-1 antitrypsin. This enzymatic imbalance degrades the elastin and collagen framework of the alveolar walls, leading to their progressive breakdown and coalescence into larger, non-functional air spaces. As a direct consequence, the total surface area available for respiratory gas exchange is severely compromised.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
In patients suffering from emphysema, the structural damage primarily involves the alveolar walls.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER17_MCQ_Q10 - Brain centre that reduces inspiratory duration

questiontext.text: Respiratory process is regulated by certain specialized centres in the brain. One of the following centres can reduce the inspiratory duration upon stimulation

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The neural control of breathing is mediated by groups of neurons organized into respiratory centres situated in the brainstem, which modulate the rate and depth of respiration.

Step 2: Functional Role of the Centres
The respiratory rhythm centre located in the medulla oblongata generates the primary inspiratory drive. The pneumotaxic centre, situated dorsally in the upper pons, transmits inhibitory signals to this medullary rhythm centre. When stimulated, the pneumotaxic centre curtails the duration of the inspiratory ramp signal, thereby switching off inspiration earlier. This reduction in the duration of inspiration prevents overinflation of the lungs and subsequently increases the respiratory rate.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The specialized neural centre that reduces inspiratory duration upon stimulation is the pneumotaxic centre.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER17_MCQ_Q11 - Conditions for dissociation of carbamino haemoglobin

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Approximately 20 to 25 percent of carbon dioxide in the blood is transported in reversible combination with the globin amine groups of haemoglobin as carbaminohaemoglobin.

Step 2: Evaluation of Gas Exchange Conditions
The binding and dissociation of carbon dioxide with haemoglobin depend predominantly on the relative partial pressures of \(\text{CO}_2\) and \(\text{O}_2\). In peripheral tissues, high \(\text{pCO}_2\) and low \(\text{pO}_2\) favour the formation of carbaminohaemoglobin. When venous blood reaches the pulmonary capillaries of the alveoli, it encounters high \(\text{pO}_2\) and low \(\text{pCO}_2\). Under these conditions, oxygen binds cooperatively with haemoglobin, which alters the conformation of the protein and markedly reduces its affinity for carbon dioxide, thereby promoting the rapid dissociation of \(\text{CO}_2\) from carbaminohaemoglobin into the alveoli for exhalation.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Carbon dioxide dissociates from carbaminohaemoglobin under conditions where \(\text{pO}_2\) is high and \(\text{pCO}_2\) is low.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER17_MCQ_Q12 - Estimation of air volume during breathing

questiontext.text: In breathing movements, air volume can be estimated by

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Different clinical diagnostic instruments are designed to quantify specific physiological activities and parameters in the human body.

Step 2: Evaluation of Instruments
A stethoscope is used to detect and amplify internal sounds produced by the heart, lungs, and bowels. A hygrometer is an instrument used in meteorology and physical sciences to measure the humidity or moisture content of air. A sphygmomanometer is designed to measure systemic arterial blood pressure. A spirometer is a dedicated medical device utilized to record and quantify the volumes of air inspired and expired during quiet and forced respiratory cycles, assisting in clinical pulmonary function testing.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The volume of air involved in breathing movements is estimated using a spirometer.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER17_MCQ_Q13 - Relationships between respiratory volumes and capacities

questiontext.text:
From the following relationships between respiratory volume and capacities and mark the correct answer

i. Inspiratory capacity (IC) = Tidal Volume + Residual Volume
ii. Vital Capacity (VC) = Tidal Volume (TV) + Inspiratory Reserve Volume (IRV) + Expiratory Reserve Volume (ERV).
iii. Residual Volume (RV) = Vital Capacity (VC) – Inspiratory Reserve Volume (IRV)
iv. Tidal Volume (TV) = Inspiratory Capacity (IC) – Inspiratory Reserve Volume (IRV)

Options:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Relevant Definitions and Formulae
Respiratory capacities are mathematical sums of specific primary respiratory volumes:
Inspiratory Capacity: \(\text{IC} = \text{TV} + \text{IRV}\)
Vital Capacity: \(\text{VC} = \text{TV} + \text{IRV} + \text{ERV}\)
Total Lung Capacity: \(\text{TLC} = \text{VC} + \text{RV}\)

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Relationship
The relationship defining Inspiratory Capacity as the sum of Tidal Volume and Residual Volume is incorrect, because Inspiratory Capacity is the sum of Tidal Volume and Inspiratory Reserve Volume.
The relationship defining Vital Capacity as the sum of Tidal Volume, Inspiratory Reserve Volume, and Expiratory Reserve Volume is correct.
The relationship defining Residual Volume as Vital Capacity minus Inspiratory Reserve Volume is incorrect, because subtracting Inspiratory Reserve Volume from Vital Capacity yields Tidal Volume plus Expiratory Reserve Volume (which corresponds to Expiratory Capacity), not Residual Volume.
Rearranging the formula for Inspiratory Capacity (\(\text{IC} = \text{TV} + \text{IRV}\)) yields \(\text{TV} = \text{IC} - \text{IRV}\), which is correct.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The first and third relationships are incorrect, while the second and fourth relationships are correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER17_MCQ_Q14 - Factors causing right shift in curve

questiontext.text: The oxygen - haemoglobin dissociation curve will show a right shift in case of

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The oxygen-haemoglobin dissociation curve is a sigmoid curve relating the percentage saturation of haemoglobin to the partial pressure of oxygen. A shift of this curve to the right denotes a decreased affinity of haemoglobin for oxygen, thereby promoting the dissociation and release of oxygen to metabolically active tissues.

Step 2: Factors Modulating the Dissociation Curve
A shift of the curve to the right (the Bohr effect) is induced by physiological conditions indicative of high tissue metabolism, namely increased \(\text{pCO}_2\), increased hydrogen ion concentration (\(\text{H}^+\) concentration, or lower pH), elevated temperature, and increased 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate concentration. Conversely, high \(\text{pO}_2\), low \(\text{pCO}_2\), lower \(\text{H}^+\) concentration (higher pH), and lower temperature increase haemoglobin's affinity for oxygen, shifting the curve to the left.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
A rightward shift of the oxygen-haemoglobin dissociation curve occurs under conditions of high \(\text{pCO}_2\).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER17_MCQ_Q15 - Matching animals with their respiratory organs

questiontext.text:
Match the following and mark the correct options

Animal Respiratory Organ
A. Earthworm i. Moist cuticle
B. Insects ii. Gills
C. Fishes iii. Lungs
D. Birds/Reptiles iv. Trachea

Options:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Different animal phyla have evolved specialized respiratory structures and mechanisms adapted to their specific ecological habitats and levels of structural organization.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Organism
Earthworms (annelids) possess a vascularized body wall and respire through cutaneous diffusion across their moist cuticle.
Insects (terrestrial arthropods) utilize a complex internal network of air tubes termed a tracheal system for direct gas exchange.
Fishes (aquatic vertebrates) rely on vascularized filamentous gills to absorb oxygen dissolved in water.
Birds and reptiles (terrestrial vertebrates) possess highly vascularized, spongy lungs to perform pulmonary respiration.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Matching each animal to its corresponding respiratory organ yields Earthworm with moist cuticle, Insects with trachea, Fishes with gills, and Birds/Reptiles with lungs (A-i, B-iv, C-ii, D-iii).
